claims.text: The target alloy is a single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloy such as HfNbTaTiZr, initially in a disordered or weakly ordered state at elevated temperature.
Controlled annealing or thermal cycling can evolve SRO clusters until they form a connected, percolating network.
SRO is thermodynamically stable in the approximate range 0.5 Tm to 0.8 Tm while the alloy remains single-phase bcc.

Percolating SRO clusters will cause an anomalous increase in thermal conductivity, or a substantially smaller decrease than conventional scattering models predict, relative to a random solid solution.
A percolating SRO network acts as a coherent phonon-transport channel.
In the dilute-SRO regime, phonons scatter from individual SRO clusters, reducing thermal conductivity.
Percolation of SRO clusters makes the local potential-energy landscape spatially correlated.
The SRO network can have a smoother or more coherent potential-energy surface than the random-alloy background because it has reduced chemical disorder.
Phonons can propagate along the connected SRO network with reduced scattering, producing a phonon-wire-like effect.
The connected low-scattering pathway bypasses localized scattering centers that dominate when SRO clusters are dilute.
Series/parallel mixing and Callaway-type models fail in this regime because they treat SRO as isolated or uncorrelated scatterers rather than as a connected structural mediator.
The interatomic potential must permit stable percolating SRO without macroscopic phase separation.
Standard interatomic potentials often predict SRO evolution incorrectly because they inadequately represent multibody interactions in disordered alloys.
The conductivity transition will be sharp and occur at a critical SRO volume fraction corresponding to the percolation threshold.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains single-phase bcc and does not form B2, Laves, amorphous, or other macroscopic secondary structures.
The mechanism is invalid when SRO clusters remain isolated or when the SRO-network potential-energy surface is too rough to support coherent phonon transport.
The exact percolation threshold and conductivity change depend critically on the interatomic potential used to model SRO evolution.
Highly dynamic SRO clusters may broaden the conductivity transition rather than produce a sharp transition.
APT-derived SRO connectivity can be correlated with thermal-conductivity measurements to test whether a conductivity anomaly coincides with percolation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome states that the transition will be sharp, whereas the uncertainty field allows that it may be broad rather than sharp.

The hypothesis permits a significantly smaller reduction in conductivity, which could still be monotonic, but the falsification rule declares any monotonic decrease with increasing SRO connectivity to be falsifying.
